teaser: A friar painted this at the top of a staircase, for men who passed it every single day.
review_notes:
David Hockney, 'Annunciation 2, after Fra Angelico' (2017), part of 'The Brass Tacks Triptych': title and date worth confirming.
This is the fresco at the top of the dormitory stairs (north corridor) of San Marco, about 230 x 321 cm; usually dated c. 1440-1445 (metadata says 1443).
Cosimo de' Medici financed the rebuilding by Michelozzo and kept a cell for his own retreats.
Inscription read as 'Virginis intacte cum veneris ante figuram pretereundo cave ne sileatur ave'; translation paraphrased.
Born Guido di Pietro, in religion Fra Giovanni da Fiesole; beatified 1982, declared patron of artists 1984 by John Paul II.
Vasari's claims (prayer before painting, never retouching) are tradition, presented as such.
'More than forty cells' with frescoes by Angelico and assistants.

lesson.text: In 2017 David Hockney, the English painter famous for California swimming pools, made a picture in hot blues and oranges of two arches, an angel and a seated woman. He named his source in the title: Fra Angelico. Nearly six centuries on, a friar's wall painting was still worth borrowing.

The original is not in a gallery room. It sits at the top of a staircase in San Marco, a convent in Florence, on the corridor leading to the friars' bedrooms. It is about 3.2 meters wide (10.5 feet). Climb the stairs and it rises over you step by step, the figures close to life size.
The convent had just been rebuilt with money from Cosimo de' Medici, the banker who ran Florence. He kept a cell there for himself, a place to retreat from business and pray among the friars.

The subject is the Annunciation: the angel Gabriel tells Mary she will bear the son of God. Painters usually loaded it with props. A white lily, a dove, a prayer book, rays of gold. Fra Angelico leaves almost all of it out. What remains is two figures, and what they do with their arms.

lesson.title: Two bows
lesson.text: Start with the angel on the left, then cross the column to Mary.

spots.title: The angel's arms
spots.text: Gabriel has just landed, one knee bending, and crosses his forearms over his chest. No pointing finger, no scroll of words. The messenger of God greets a young woman with a gesture of respect.

spots.title: The same gesture
spots.text: Mary answers by crossing her own arms the same way and leaning forward. The two bodies mirror each other across the column, like a question and its reply.

spots.title: Her face
spots.text: Eyes wide, lips closed, head tilted toward the visitor. She looks startled and attentive at once. The halo behind her is a plain disc scratched with fine rays.

spots.title: The stool
spots.text: No throne, no cushion: a rough wooden stool with splayed legs. The future Queen of Heaven sits on the kind of furniture a friar might have in his cell.

lesson.text: Crossed arms meant humility and acceptance. That matching gesture is the whole event: an offer made gently, and a yes. The painter knew his audience. They were Dominican friars, who had promised to live poor and obedient, and who walked past this wall on the way to bed and on the way to prayers.
Fra Angelico strips a famous story down to a greeting between two people. The picture was made to slow a passerby into prayer, so it stays as plain and quiet as the life around it.

He was one of them. Born Guido di Pietro, he became Brother Giovanni when he joined the order. “Fra Angelico,” the angelic brother, is a nickname that stuck after his death. With his assistants he painted a scene in each of more than forty cells along these corridors, one for every friar to live with.

The porch is modern for the 1440s: round arches, slim columns, depth drawn with the new science of perspective, the method for making a flat surface look deep. It resembles the cloister just built downstairs. Behind Mary the porch opens onto a bare little room, and that room has a single way of seeing out.
The room behind Mary is as empty as a friar's cell. Where is its one opening to the outside?

spots.title: The barred window
spots.text: A small square window crossed by bars, with a patch of green beyond. It is the deepest point of the picture, and it turns Mary's home into a cell like the ones that open off this very corridor.

lesson.text: So the friars saw their own rooms in her room, and their own cloister in her porch. On the other side, a wooden fence closes off a garden thick with small flowers. A fenced garden was an old emblem of Mary's purity, but it is also simply a convent garden, shut off from the city.
A line of Latin runs along the bottom edge, addressed to whoever walks by. It says, roughly: when you come before the image of the Virgin, take care that you do not pass without saying a Hail Mary.

The perspective is not strict, and you can test it. Imagine Mary standing up: her head would hit the vault. Fra Angelico used the new geometry as far as it helped him and no further. He cared more that the two figures feel close than that every column measures correctly.

An early biographer, Giorgio Vasari, wrote that Fra Angelico never picked up a brush without first saying a prayer, and never went back to correct a figure, believing the first version was the one God intended.

In 1982 the Catholic Church gave the nickname some official weight by beatifying him, a step toward sainthood, and soon after named him patron of artists. The fresco is still at the top of the stairs. Hockney kept its arches and changed nearly everything else. Would you have kept the same things?

quiz.question: Where in the convent is this fresco?
options: Behind the main altar of the church
At the top of the stairs to the friars' cells
quiz.explanation: It faces the staircase on the corridor that leads to the friars' rooms.

quiz.question: What gesture do the angel and Mary share?
quiz.explanation: Both cross their arms, a sign of humility and acceptance.

quiz.question: What does Mary sit on?
quiz.explanation: A rough stool, as simple as a friar's furniture.

quiz.question: What does the Latin inscription at the bottom ask of passersby?
options: To give money to the convent
quiz.explanation: It reminds anyone passing not to forget to say a Hail Mary.

quiz.question: What was Fra Angelico's name at birth?
quiz.explanation: He was born Guido di Pietro and became Brother Giovanni as a friar.

facts.text: “Fra Angelico” was a nickname that became standard after the painter's death.
facts.explanation: In life he was Brother Giovanni; “the angelic brother” came later.

facts.text: The fresco is full of traditional props such as a lily, a dove and a prayer book.
facts.explanation: Fra Angelico left those out and kept only the two figures and their gestures.

facts.text: The perspective is so exact that Mary could stand up comfortably under the vault.
facts.explanation: If she stood, her head would hit the ceiling; the geometry is loose on purpose.
